title: Φυγὰς καὶ πτωχός
titleEn: The Exile’s Passage and the Beggar’s Plan — Odyssey 15.260–350
part: The Exile’s Passage and the Beggar’s Plan (15.260–350)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Theoclymenus, who has come up to Telemachus at the ship, asks him who he is and begs to be taken on board: he has killed a man of his own tribe and is fleeing the dead man's many kinsmen. Telemachus takes him aboard, the crew sets the mast and sail, and Athena sends a fair wind; the ship runs past Crouni and Chalcis, Pheae and Elis, and toward the swift islands, with Telemachus unsure whether he will escape death. Back in the hut, after supper, Odysseus in his beggar's guise says he will go to the town at dawn to beg, carry news to Penelope and wait on the suitors, and tests the swineherd with the plan. Eumaeus is dismayed, describes the suitors' violence and their well-dressed servants, and bids him stay until Telemachus returns. Odysseus thanks him, says there is nothing worse for mortals than roaming, and asks whether the mother and father of Odysseus are still alive.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλ’, ἐπεί σε θύοντα κιχάνω τῷδ’ ἐνὶ χώρῳ,
λίσσομ’ ὑπὲρ θυέων καὶ δαίμονος, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
σῆς τ’ αὐτοῦ κεφαλῆς καὶ ἑταίρων, οἵ τοι ἕπονται,
εἰπέ μοι εἰρομένῳ νημερτέα μηδ’ ἐπικεύσῃς·
sentences.tr:
ō phil’, epei se thyonta kichanō tōid’ eni chōrōi,
lissom’ hyper thyeōn kai daimonos, autar epeita
sēs t’ autou kephalēs kai hetairōn, hoi toi hepontai,
eipe moi eiromenōi nēmertea mēd’ epikeusēis·
sentences.l:
“O friend, since sacrificing I come upon you in this place,
I entreat you by the sacrifices and by a power, and then
by your own head and by your companions, who follow you,
tell me, asking, unerring things, and do not conceal them;
sentences.i: “Friend, since I find you sacrificing in this place, I entreat you by the sacrifices and by some power, and then by your own head and by the companions who follow you: tell me, as I ask, unerring things, and do not conceal them;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλ’ is the vocative of φίλος 'friend' (φίλε elided). κιχάνω 'come upon, find' takes the participle θύοντα, so 'since I find you sacrificing'. λίσσομ’ is λίσσομαι 'entreat'; ὑπέρ with the genitive means 'in the name of', so the entreaty is made by the sacrifices (θυέων), by a power (δαίμονος, the divine power to whom the sacrifices are made, left unnamed), and by Telemachus's own head (κεφαλῆς), an oath-like phrase in which the head stands for the person. οἵ τοι ἕπονται: τοι is the dative of σύ, 'who follow you'. εἰρομένῳ is a dative participle of εἴρομαι 'ask', agreeing with μοι, 'as I ask'. νημερτέα, 'unerring', is the plain truth; μηδ’ ἐπικεύσῃς is a prohibition in the aorist subjunctive, 'and do not conceal'. This is the first speech of Theoclymenus, the stranger who came up to Telemachus in the last part.

sentences.t: τίς πόθεν εἶς ἀνδρῶν;
sentences.tr: tis pothen eis andrōn;
sentences.l: Who among men are you, and from where?
sentences.i: Who among men are you, and where from?
sentences.n: τίς 'who' and πόθεν 'from where' are the two halves of the question; εἶς is the second person singular of εἰμί, 'you are' (Attic εἶ, which Homer can also print εἰς). ἀνδρῶν is a partitive genitive, 'among men'. A stranger is asked first who he is and where he comes from, before anything else is said to him.

sentences.t: πόθι τοι πόλις ἠδὲ τοκῆες;
sentences.tr: pothi toi polis ēde tokēes;
sentences.l: Where is your city and your parents?
sentences.i: Where is your city, and where are your parents?
sentences.n: πόθι 'where' has the suffix -θι of place. τοι is the dative of σύ, 'your'; ἠδέ is 'and'; τοκῆες is 'parents' (τοκεύς, from the root of τίκτω 'beget'). With these two questions the speech ends. Theoclymenus’ speech ends with this question; the closing quotation mark is left off this unit because the identical unit is shipped elsewhere without one.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖ … ἀντίον ηὔδα is a reply-formula: τόν is the pronoun 'him', αὖ 'in turn', ἀντίον 'face to face', and ηὔδα the imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak'. πεπνυμένος 'prudent' is Telemachus's standing epithet and is translated the same way each time.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι, ξεῖνε, μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως ἀγορεύσω.
sentences.tr: toigar egō toi, xeine, mal’ atrekeōs agoreusō.
sentences.l: “Well then, I will tell you, stranger, very exactly.
sentences.i: “Then I will tell you, stranger, quite exactly.
sentences.n: τοιγάρ is 'well then, accordingly'. ἀτρεκέως is an adverb, 'exactly, without error'. ἀγορεύσω is the future of ἀγορεύω 'say, tell' (the verb also underlies ἀγορή 'assembly'). ξεῖνε is the vocative of ξεῖνος, a word that means both 'stranger' and 'guest', and so is the right address to an unknown arrival who has asked for help.

sentences.t:
ἐξ Ἰθάκης γένος εἰμί, πατὴρ δέ μοί ἐστιν Ὀδυσσεύς,
εἴ ποτ’ ἔην·
sentences.tr:
ex Ithakēs genos eimi, patēr de moi estin Odysseus,
ei pot’ eēn·
sentences.l:
From Ithaca in birth I am, and father to me is Odysseus,
if ever he was;
sentences.i: I am Ithacan by birth, and my father is Odysseus, if ever he was;
sentences.n: γένος is an accusative of respect, 'in birth': ἐξ Ἰθάκης γένος εἰμί is 'I am by birth from Ithaca'. πατὴρ δέ μοί ἐστιν puts the possessor in the dative, 'to me is a father', as Greek commonly does. εἴ ποτ’ ἔην is 'if ever he was': ἔην is a Homeric imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦν). The words concede that Telemachus can no longer say whether his father lived, and the next unit goes further.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἤδη ἀπέφθιτο λυγρῷ ὀλέθρῳ.
sentences.tr: nyn d’ ēdē apephthito lygrōi olethrōi.
sentences.l: but now he has already perished by a grievous destruction.
sentences.i: but now he has already perished by a grievous destruction.
sentences.n: ἀπέφθιτο is the aorist middle of ἀποφθίνω 'waste away, perish'. ὀλέθρῳ is a dative of means, 'by destruction', with λυγρῷ 'grievous', the house word for λυγρός. νῦν δ’ ἤδη gives the contrast 'but now already'.

sentences.t:
τοὔνεκα νῦν ἑτάρους τε λαβὼν καὶ νῆα μέλαιναν
ἦλθον πευσόμενος πατρὸς δὴν οἰχομένοιο.
sentences.tr:
touneka nyn hetarous te labōn kai nēa melainan
ēlthon peusomenos patros dēn oichomenoio.
sentences.l:
For this reason now, both companions and a black ship having taken,
I came, to learn of my father, long gone.”
sentences.i: That is why I have now taken my companions and a black ship and come to find out about my father, who has long been gone.”
sentences.n: τοὔνεκα is τοῦ ἕνεκα 'for that reason'. λαβών, the aorist participle of λαμβάνω, governs both ἑτάρους and νῆα μέλαιναν; μέλαιναν 'black' is a colour-word used of ships. πευσόμενος is a future participle of πυνθάνομαι 'learn by asking', expressing purpose, with the genitive πατρός 'about my father'. δὴν οἰχομένοιο is 'long gone': δήν 'for a long time', οἰχομένοιο from οἴχομαι 'be gone', in the genitive in -οιο agreeing with πατρός. This unit ends Telemachus's speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Θεοκλύμενος θεοειδής·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe Theoklymenos theoeidēs·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Theoclymenus, godlike-in-form:
sentences.i: Then Theoclymenus, godlike in form, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is the reply-formula 'and in turn addressed him': τόν is the pronoun 'him', αὖτε 'in turn', προσέειπε the aorist of προσεῖπον 'address', with the stretched form -ειπε. Θεοκλύμενος θεοειδής: the epithet θεοειδής (θεός + εἶδος 'form') is translated 'godlike in form' every time.

sentences.t:
οὕτω τοι καὶ ἐγὼν ἐκ πατρίδος, ἄνδρα κατακτὰς
ἔμφυλον·
sentences.tr:
houtō toi kai egōn ek patridos, andra kataktas
emphylon·
sentences.l:
“Thus, you see, I too, from my fatherland, a man having killed
of the same tribe;
sentences.i: “It is so with me too: I am away from my fatherland, having killed a man of my own tribe;
sentences.n: The first clause has no verb: οὕτω τοι καὶ ἐγών ἐκ πατρίδος is 'so, you see, I too (am) from my fatherland', the English supplies 'I am away', and the verb φεύγω does not come until 276, in the next sentence. οὕτω is 'so, in this way'; τοι here is the particle 'you see', not 'to you'; ἐγών is ἐγώ before a vowel. κατακτάς is the short-stem aorist participle of κατακτείνω 'kill' (the Attic equivalent is κατακτανών). ἔμφυλος means 'of the same tribe', so the dead man was a kinsman. The unit stops in the middle of line 273 at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ δὲ κασίγνητοί τε ἔται τε
Ἄργος ἀν’ ἱππόβοτον, μέγα δὲ κρατέουσιν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
polloi de kasignētoi te etai te
Argos an’ hippoboton, mega de krateousin Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
and many there are, both brothers and kinsmen,
throughout horse-pasturing Argos, and greatly they hold sway over Achaeans.
sentences.i: and many are his brothers and kinsmen throughout horse-pasturing Argos, and they hold great sway over the Achaeans.
sentences.n: The Greek gives no possessive: πολλοὶ … κασίγνητοί τε ἔται τε is 'many (are) both brothers and kinsmen', and the sense is those of the dead man. κασίγνητοι are 'brothers', ἔται 'kinsmen, clansmen'. Ἄργος ἀν’ ἱππόβοτον: ἀν’ is ἀνά 'throughout', and ἱππόβοτος 'horse-pasturing' is the epithet of Argos here; Argos here is the region of the Peloponnese, and Ἀχαιῶν 'the Achaeans' its people. μέγα is an adverb, 'greatly'; κρατέουσιν is the uncontracted form of κρατέω, which takes the genitive, 'hold sway over'.

sentences.t:
τῶν ὑπαλευάμενος θάνατον καὶ κῆρα μέλαιναν
φεύγω, ἐπεί νύ μοι αἶσα κατ’ ἀνθρώπους ἀλάλησθαι.
sentences.tr:
tōn hypaleuamenos thanaton kai kēra melainan
pheugō, epei ny moi aisa kat’ anthrōpous alalēsthai.
sentences.l:
Evading from them death and black death-fate
I flee, since indeed for me it is a portion to wander among men.
sentences.i: I am fleeing from them, avoiding death and the black spirit of death, since it is now my lot to wander among men.
sentences.n: τῶν is the pronoun 'them', the kinsmen. ὑπαλευάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ὑπαλεύομαι 'slip away from, avoid'. θάνατον and κῆρα are both its objects: κήρ is the death-spirit, a power that brings death, and is a different word from κῆρ 'heart'; μέλαιναν is 'black'. φεύγω is the present 'I flee'. ἐπεί νύ μοι αἶσα has no verb: 'since to me (is) a portion'; αἶσα 'portion, allotted share'. ἀλάλησθαι is the perfect infinitive of ἀλάομαι 'wander', 'to be a wanderer'; κατ’ ἀνθρώπους 'among men'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά με νηὸς ἔφεσσαι, ἐπεί σε φυγὼν ἱκέτευσα,
μή με κατακτείνωσι·
sentences.tr:
alla me nēos ephessai, epei se phygōn hiketeusa,
mē me katakteinōsi·
sentences.l:
But set me on a ship, since fleeing I supplicated you,
lest they kill me;
sentences.i: But take me on board, since I have fled and made my plea to you as a suppliant, so that they may not kill me;
sentences.n: ἔφεσσαι is the aorist imperative middle of ἐφέζω in its causative sense, 'seat, set on board'; με is its object and νηός a genitive, 'on a ship'. φυγών is the aorist participle of φεύγω 'flee', and ἱκέτευσα the aorist of ἱκετεύω 'approach as a suppliant'; the aorist marks the act as done, 'I have come to you as a suppliant'. μή με κατακτείνωσι is a clause with μή and the aorist subjunctive, 'lest they kill me', the subject being the dead man's kinsmen. The unit stops in the middle of line 278.

sentences.t: διωκέμεναι γὰρ ὀΐω.
sentences.tr: diōkemenai gar oïō.
sentences.l: for they are pursuing, I suppose.”
sentences.i: for I suppose they are in pursuit.”
sentences.n: διωκέμεναι is an infinitive in -έμεναι of διώκω 'pursue'; the subject is not named. ὀΐω is the first person of ὀΐομαι 'suppose, expect', with an infinitive, 'I suppose (them) to be pursuing'. γάρ gives the reason for the fear in the clause before. This unit ends the speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This is the same line as 265: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα. Homer repeats his introductory formulas word for word, and the English repeats too, so that the reader can hear it.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν δή σ’ ἐθέλοντά γ’ ἀπώσω νηὸς ἐΐσης,
ἀλλ’ ἕπευ·
sentences.tr:
ou men dē s’ ethelonta g’ apōsō nēos eïsēs,
all’ hepeu·
sentences.l:
“Not indeed will I thrust you, being willing, away from the well-balanced ship,
but follow;
sentences.i: “I will certainly not thrust you, willing as you are, away from the well-balanced ship, but come along with us;
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν δή is 'certainly not'. ἐθέλοντα is a participle agreeing with σ’ (σε), 'you who are willing'. ἀπώσω is a future of ἀπωθέω 'thrust away', with the genitive of separation νηὸς ἐΐσης 'from the ship'. ἐΐσης 'well-balanced' is the traditional rendering of an adjective whose sense is not certain; it means 'even, equal' and is the usual epithet of a ship. ἕπευ is the imperative of ἕπομαι 'follow'.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ κεῖθι φιλήσεαι, οἷά κ’ ἔχωμεν.
sentences.tr: autar keithi philēseai, hoia k’ echōmen.
sentences.l: but there you will be welcomed, with such things as we may have.”
sentences.i: and there you will be made welcome with whatever we have.”
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is 'but, and'; κεῖθι is 'there', the adverb with -θι of place (Attic ἐκεῖ). φιλήσεαι is a future middle of φιλέω with passive sense, 'you will be treated as a friend, welcomed', in the uncontracted ending -εαι. οἷά κ’ ἔχωμεν is a relative clause with κε and the subjunctive, 'such things as we may have': the welcome promised is only as good as what the ship has. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας οἱ ἐδέξατο χάλκεον ἔγχος,
καὶ τό γ’ ἐπ’ ἰκριόφιν τάνυσεν νεὸς ἀμφιελίσσης·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsas hoi edexato chalkeon enchos,
kai to g’ ep’ ikriophin tanysen neos amphielissēs·
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, from him he received the bronze spear,
and it onto the decking he stretched, of the both-sides-curving ship;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and took the bronze spear from him, and laid it at full length on the decking of the ship curved on both sides;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is 'so then having spoken', here with a masculine participle: Telemachus is the subject throughout. ἐδέξατο is the aorist middle of δέχομαι 'receive'; οἱ is a dative of the person from whom, 'from him', so Theoclymenus hands over his spear before boarding. ἔγχος 'spear' with χάλκεον 'bronze'. ἰκριόφιν is ἴκρια, the ship's decking, with the suffix -φιν, which does the work of a case ending, here 'onto the decking'. τάνυσεν is the aorist of τανύω 'stretch, lay at full length'. νεὸς ἀμφιελίσσης: ἀμφιέλισσα 'curved on both sides' is the traditional sense of a ship's epithet that is disputed ('rowed on both sides' is also guessed).

sentences.t: ἂν δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς νηὸς ἐβήσετο ποντοπόροιο.
sentences.tr: an de kai autos nēos ebēseto pontoporoio.
sentences.l: and up also he himself went onto the sea-crossing ship.
sentences.i: and he himself too went aboard the sea-crossing ship.
sentences.n: ἂν is ἀνά, standing apart from its verb in tmesis: ἀνεβήσετο, 'went up onto, boarded', with the genitive νηός. ἐβήσετο is a middle aorist of βαίνω. αὐτός 'he himself' is Telemachus, as after the spear is stowed. ποντοπόροιο, 'sea-crossing' (πόντος 'open sea' + πόρος 'passage'), is the epithet of the ship here.

sentences.t:
ἐν πρύμνῃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα καθέζετο, πὰρ δὲ οἷ αὐτῷ
εἷσε Θεοκλύμενον·
sentences.tr:
en prymnēi d’ ar’ epeita kathezeto, par de hoi autōi
heise Theoklymenon·
sentences.l:
In the stern then thereupon he sat down, and close beside him
he seated Theoclymenus;
sentences.i: He sat down in the stern, and seated Theoclymenus close beside him;
sentences.n: ἐν πρύμνῃ is 'in the stern' (πρύμνη, the hindmost part of the ship); καθέζετο is 'sat down'. πὰρ δὲ οἷ αὐτῷ: πάρ is παρά 'beside', and οἷ αὐτῷ is the dative of the third-person pronoun, here reflexive, 'to himself', with αὐτῷ emphasising it ('right beside him'); English 'beside himself' would mean something else, so the sense is given. εἷσε is the aorist of ἵζω in its transitive sense, 'caused to sit, seated'.

sentences.t: τοὶ δὲ πρυμνήσι’ ἔλυσαν.
sentences.tr: toi de prymnēsi’ elysan.
sentences.l: and they loosed the stern-cables.
sentences.i: and they cast off the stern-cables.
sentences.n: τοί is the pronoun 'they' (Attic οἱ), the companions. πρυμνήσια are the stern-cables, the lines that held the ship by its stern to the shore; loosing them is the act of casting off. ἔλυσαν is the aorist of λύω 'loose'.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἑτάροισιν ἐποτρύνας ἐκέλευσεν
ὅπλων ἅπτεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
Tēlemachos d’ hetaroisin epotrynas ekeleusen
hoplōn haptesthai·
sentences.l:
And Telemachus, having urged on his comrades, commanded them
to lay hold of the tackle;
sentences.i: And Telemachus urged his comrades on and ordered them to take hold of the ship's gear;
sentences.n: ἐποτρύνας is the aorist participle of ἐποτρύνω 'urge on', and ἐκέλευσεν 'ordered' is the main verb, the dative ἑτάροισιν 'the comrades' going with the urging, and the same men understood as those ordered. ὅπλων is a genitive, as verbs of taking hold require: ἅπτεσθαι ὅπλων is 'to take hold of the tackle'. ὅπλα in the plural is a ship's gear in general, not weapons.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ἐσσυμένως ἐπίθοντο.
sentences.tr: toi d’ essymenōs epithonto.
sentences.l: and they eagerly obeyed.
sentences.i: and they obeyed eagerly.
sentences.n: τοί is again 'they', the crew. ἐσσυμένως is an adverb from ἔσσυμαι, the perfect of σεύομαι 'hurry', 'in haste, eagerly'. ἐπίθοντο is the aorist middle of πείθω, which in the middle means 'obey'.

sentences.t:
ἱστὸν δ’ εἰλάτινον κοίλης ἔντοσθε μεσόδμης
στῆσαν ἀείραντες, κατὰ δὲ προτόνοισιν ἔδησαν,
ἕλκον δ’ ἱστία λευκὰ ἐϋστρέπτοισι βοεῦσι.
sentences.tr:
histon d’ eilatinon koilēs entosthe mesodmēs
stēsan aeirantes, kata de protonoisin edēsan,
helkon d’ histia leuka eÿstreptoisi boeusi.
sentences.l:
And the mast, of fir, within the hollow mast-block
they set up, having raised it, and down with the forestays they bound it,
and they hauled up the white sails with well-twisted oxhide ropes.
sentences.i: They raised the fir mast and set it in the hollow mast-block, and made it fast with the forestays, and hauled up the white sails with well-twisted ropes of oxhide.
sentences.n: ἱστόν 'mast' is the object of both στῆσαν and ἔδησαν; ἱστός also means a weaver's loom. εἰλάτινον 'of fir'. μεσόδμη is the mast-block, the housing that holds the foot of the mast; ἔντοσθε 'within'. στῆσαν is a transitive aorist of ἵστημι (Attic ἔστησαν) and ἀείραντες the aorist participle of ἀείρω 'raise': 'having raised it, they set it up'. κατὰ δὲ προτόνοισιν ἔδησαν is tmesis, κατέδησαν 'bound down', with the forestays, the ropes that hold the mast forward. ἕλκον is the imperfect 'hauled', ἱστία 'sails'; ἐϋστρέπτοισι βοεῦσι is a dative plural, 'with well-twisted ropes of oxhide' (βοῦς 'ox' stands for its hide).

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ ἴκμενον οὖρον ἵει γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
λάβρον ἐπαιγίζοντα δι’ αἰθέρος, ὄφρα τάχιστα
νηῦς ἀνύσειε θέουσα θαλάσσης ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr:
toisin d’ ikmenon ouron hiei glaukōpis Athēnē,
labron epaigizonta di’ aitheros, ophra tachista
nēus anyseie theousa thalassēs halmyron hydōr.
sentences.l:
And for them a favorable wind sent gleaming-eyed Athena,
violent, rushing-upon through the upper air, so that most quickly
the ship might accomplish, running, the salt water of the sea.
sentences.i: And gleaming-eyed Athena sent them a favoring wind, a violent one, rushing on through the upper air, so that the ship might finish her run over the salt water of the sea as quickly as possible.
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is the dative 'for them'; ἵει is the imperfect of ἵημι 'send'; the wind that Athena sends is οὖρον, a 'fair wind'. ἴκμενον, 'favoring', is the traditional gloss of a rare adjective whose sense is not certain. λάβρον 'violent'. ἐπαιγίζοντα is a rare verb, probably 'rushing upon', its sense taken from the context. δι’ αἰθέρος: αἰθήρ is the bright upper air. ὄφρα with the optative ἀνύσειε is a purpose clause, 'so that (the ship) might accomplish', ἀνύω 'accomplish, finish (a distance)', with θέουσα 'running' and the object θαλάσσης ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ 'the salt water of the sea'; τάχιστα 'most quickly'. γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη: the epithet is 'gleaming-eyed' wherever it stands.

sentences.t: βὰν δὲ παρὰ Κρουνοὺς καὶ Χαλκίδα καλλιρέεθρον.
sentences.tr: ban de para Krounous kai Chalkida kallireethron.
sentences.l: And they went along past Crouni and Chalcis, fair-flowing.
sentences.i: They passed Crouni and fair-flowing Chalcis.
sentences.n: βάν is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω, 'they went' (Attic ἔβησαν); παρά with the accusative 'along, past'. Κρουνούς 'Crouni' (the name means 'Springs') and Χαλκίδα are places passed on the course. καλλιρέεθρον 'fair-flowing' (καλλι- 'fair' + ῥέεθρον 'stream') is the epithet of Chalcis here.

sentences.t: δύσετό τ’ ἠέλιος σκιόωντό τε πᾶσαι ἀγυιαί·
sentences.tr: dyseto t’ ēelios skioōnto te pasai aguiai·
sentences.l: And the sun set, and all the streets grew shadowy.
sentences.i: The sun set, and all the streets grew dark.
sentences.n: δύσετο is the unaugmented aorist middle of δύω 'sink', the verb for a setting sun; ἠέλιος is the Ionic form of ἥλιος 'sun'. σκιόωντο is the imperfect of σκιάομαι 'be shadowed' with the stretched vowel. ἀγυιαί 'streets' belongs to this stock evening line. The unit ends at the ano teleia, and the course of the ship goes on in the next.

sentences.t:
ἡ δὲ Φεὰς ἐπέβαλλεν ἐπειγομένη Διὸς οὔρῳ
ἠδὲ παρ’ Ἤλιδα δῖαν, ὅθι κρατέουσιν Ἐπειοί.
sentences.tr:
hē de Pheas epeballen epeigomenē Dios ourōi
ēde par’ Ēlida dian, hothi krateousin Epeioi.
sentences.l:
And she Pheae was making for, pressed on by the fair wind of Zeus,
and past heavenly Elis, where the Epeans hold sway.
sentences.i: She made for Pheae, pressed on by the fair wind of Zeus, and on past heavenly Elis, where the Epeans hold sway.
sentences.n: ἡ δέ 'and she' is the ship (νηῦς, understood). Φεάς is the accusative of Φεαί, 'Pheae', a place name, with ἐπέβαλλεν, the imperfect of ἐπιβάλλω used intransitively, 'make for'. ἐπειγομένη is 'pressed on'; Διὸς οὔρῳ is a dative of cause, 'by the fair wind of Zeus', οὖρος being a following wind. The verb is understood in ἠδὲ παρ’ Ἤλιδα δῖαν 'and past heavenly Elis': Ἤλιδα is the accusative, and δῖαν is δῖος, the epithet translated 'heavenly'. ὅθι is 'where', with -θι of place; Ἐπειοί 'the Epeans' are the people of Elis; κρατέουσιν 'hold sway' is uncontracted.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν δ’ αὖ νήσοισιν ἐπιπροέηκε θοῇσιν,
ὁρμαίνων ἤ κεν θάνατον φύγοι ἦ κεν ἁλώῃ.
sentences.tr:
enthen d’ au nēsoisin epiproeēke thoēisin,
hormainōn ē ken thanaton phygoi ē ken halōēi.
sentences.l:
And from there in turn toward the swift islands he sent her on,
pondering whether he would escape death or be taken.
sentences.i: From there he sent her on toward the swift islands, pondering whether he would escape death or be caught.
sentences.n: ἔνθεν δ’ αὖ: ἔνθεν 'from there' has the suffix -θεν; the subject is Telemachus and the object, the ship, is understood. ἐπιπροέηκε is the aorist of ἐπιπροίημι 'send on toward', with the dative νήσοισιν θοῇσιν; θοῇσιν is 'swift', and whether it is a mere epithet of the islands or part of their name is not clear. ὁρμαίνων 'pondering' introduces a double indirect question: ἤ κεν … φύγοι, optative of φεύγω 'might escape', ἦ κεν ἁλώῃ, aorist subjunctive of ἁλίσκομαι 'be taken, captured'. What he fears is not named in these lines.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ αὖτ’ ἐν κλισίῃ Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ δῖος ὑφορβὸς
δορπείτην·
sentences.tr:
tō d’ aut’ en klisiēi Odyseus kai dios hyphorbos
dorpeitēn·
sentences.l:
And the two of them in turn, in the hut, Odysseus and the heavenly swineherd,
were having supper;
sentences.i: Meanwhile, in the hut, Odysseus and the heavenly swineherd were having their supper;
sentences.n: τὼ is the dual of the pronoun, 'the two'; δορπείτην is the dual imperfect of δορπέω 'have supper' (δόρπον, the evening meal). αὖτ’ marks the change of scene, 'in turn'. κλισίη is the 'hut'. ὑφορβός 'swineherd' (ὑπό + φέρβω 'feed') is Eumaeus, here with the epithet δῖος, 'heavenly', the word that is also Odysseus's. The unit stops in the middle of line 302.

sentences.t: παρὰ δέ σφιν ἐδόρπεον ἀνέρες ἄλλοι.
sentences.tr: para de sphin edorpeon aneres alloi.
sentences.l: and beside them were having supper other men.
sentences.i: and beside them other men were having supper.
sentences.n: σφιν is the dative plural 'them'; ἐδόρπεον is the uncontracted imperfect plural of δορπέω; ἀνέρες is a form of ἄνδρες 'men'. The other men are not named.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
τοῖς δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς μετέειπε, συβώτεω πειρητίζων,
ἤ μιν ἔτ’ ἐνδυκέως φιλέοι μεῖναί τε κελεύοι
αὐτοῦ ἐνὶ σταθμῷ, ἦ ὀτρύνειε πόλινδε·
sentences.tr:
autar epei posios kai edētyos ex eron hento,
tois d’ Odyseus meteeipe, sybōteō peirētizōn,
ē min et’ endykeōs phileoi meinai te keleuoi
autou eni stathmōi, ē otryneie polinde·
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
and among them Odysseus spoke, the swineherd testing,
whether him still kindly he would welcome and would bid him stay
right there in the steading, or would urge him to the city:
sentences.i: But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, Odysseus spoke among them, testing the swineherd, to see whether he would still welcome him kindly and bid him stay right there in the steading, or would urge him to go to the city:
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο is the stock line for the end of a meal: ἔρον is 'desire', and ἕντο is from ἵημι 'send', with ἐξ in tmesis, 'sent out from them'. τοῖς … μετέειπε 'spoke among them'. συβώτεω, the genitive in -εω of συβώτης 'swineherd' (Attic συβώτου), is the object of πειρητίζων 'testing'. The question that follows has two halves, ἤ … φιλέοι … κελεύοι and ἦ ὀτρύνειε, 'whether … or', in the optative: ἔτ’ 'still', ἐνδυκέως 'kindly', φιλέοι 'would welcome' (φιλέω, treat as a friend), μεῖναι 'to stay', αὐτοῦ 'right there', σταθμῷ 'steading', ὀτρύνειε πόλινδε 'would urge him on to the city', with the -δε of direction.

sentences.t: κέκλυθι νῦν, Εὔμαιε, καὶ ἄλλοι πάντες ἑταῖροι·
sentences.tr: keklythi nyn, Eumaie, kai alloi pantes hetairoi·
sentences.l: “Hear now, Eumaeus, and all the other companions;
sentences.i: “Hear me now, Eumaeus, and all you other companions;
sentences.n: κέκλυθι is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω, 'hear!'. Εὔμαιε is the vocative of Εὔμαιος. ἄλλοι πάντες ἑταῖροι are 'all the other companions': the speech is addressed to the swineherd and the men who supped beside him. Odysseus is speaking as the beggar, and is still testing the swineherd.

sentences.t:
ἠῶθεν προτὶ ἄστυ λιλαίομαι ἀπονέεσθαι
πτωχεύσων, ἵνα μή σε κατατρύχω καὶ ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr:
ēōthen proti asty lilaiomai aponeesthai
ptōcheusōn, hina mē se katatrychō kai hetairous.
sentences.l:
At dawn to the town I long to go away,
to beg, so that I may not wear you out, and your companions.
sentences.i: At daybreak I long to go off to the town and beg, so that I may not wear out you and your companions.
sentences.n: ἠῶθεν 'at dawn' has the suffix -θεν; προτί is πρός; ἄστυ 'town'. λιλαίομαι 'long for' takes the infinitive ἀπονέεσθαι, the uncontracted form of ἀπονέομαι 'go away, go back'. πτωχεύσων is a future participle of πτωχεύω 'beg', of purpose. ἵνα μή with the subjunctive κατατρύχω gives 'so that I may not wear out', κατατρύχω being 'rub away, use up': he would be a drain on his host. καὶ ἑταίρους is a second object, 'and (your) companions'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μοι εὖ θ’ ὑπόθευ καὶ ἅμ’ ἡγεμόν’ ἐσθλὸν ὄπασσον
ὅς κέ με κεῖσ’ ἀγάγῃ·
sentences.tr:
alla moi eu th’ hypotheu kai ham’ hēgemon’ esthlon opasson
hos ke me keis’ agagēi·
sentences.l:
But for me advise well, and along with me a good leader give,
who may lead me there;
sentences.i: But advise me well, and send a good leader along with me, to take me there;
sentences.n: ὑπόθευ is the aorist imperative middle of ὑποτίθημι 'suggest, give advice'; εὖ 'well', θ’ is τε 'and'. ἡγεμών is 'leader', one who goes ahead on the way; ὄπασσον is the aorist imperative of ὀπάζω 'make follow, give as an attendant'. ὅς κέ με κεῖσ’ ἀγάγῃ is a relative clause with κε and the aorist subjunctive, 'who is to lead me there', κεῖσε 'to that place'. The unit stops in the middle of line 311.

sentences.t:
κατὰ δὲ πτόλιν αὐτὸς ἀνάγκῃ
πλάγξομαι, αἴ κέν τις κοτύλην καὶ πύρνον ὀρέξῃ.
sentences.tr:
kata de ptolin autos anankēi
planxomai, ai ken tis kotylēn kai pyrnon orexēi.
sentences.l:
and through the city I myself, of necessity,
will stray, if perhaps someone may hold out a cup and a wheaten loaf.
sentences.i: and I myself will roam through the city out of necessity, in case someone should offer a cup and a wheaten loaf.
sentences.n: πτόλιν is the older form of πόλις, 'city'; ἀνάγκῃ is a dative, 'of necessity'. πλάγξομαι is the future of πλάζω, 'be driven off course, stray'; the English keeps 'stray' and 'roam' for this word and its noun πλαγκτοσύνη (343), and 'wander' for ἀλάομαι and ἄλη. αἴ κεν is εἰ κεν 'in case, in the hope that'; ὀρέξῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ὀρέγω 'reach out, hold out'. κοτύλη is a cup, also a small measure; πύρνος is a loaf of wheat bread, a sense taken from the traditional gloss.

sentences.t:
καί κ’ ἐλθὼν πρὸς δώματ’ Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο
ἀγγελίην εἴποιμι περίφρονι Πηνελοπείῃ,
καί κε μνηστήρεσσιν ὑπερφιάλοισι μιγείην,
εἴ μοι δεῖπνον δοῖεν ὀνείατα μυρί’ ἔχοντες.
sentences.tr:
kai k’ elthōn pros dōmat’ Odyssēos theioio
angeliēn eipoimi periphroni Pēnelopeiēi,
kai ke mnēstēressin hyperphialoisi migeiēn,
ei moi deipnon doien oneiata myri’ echontes.
sentences.l:
And I might, having gone to the house of divine Odysseus,
tell news to circumspect Penelope,
and I might mingle with the overweening suitors,
if to me a meal they would give, having dainties numberless.
sentences.i: And I might go to the house of divine Odysseus and bring news to circumspect Penelope, and I might mingle with the overweening suitors, if they, who have countless delicacies, would give me a meal.
sentences.n: εἴποιμι and μιγείην are optatives with κε, 'I might say', 'I might mingle'; ἐλθών 'having gone'. Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο is the genitive 'of divine Odysseus', with θεῖος 'divine': the beggar speaks of Odysseus as of someone else, so the words are Odysseus talking about himself. ἀγγελίην 'news, tidings' is the object of εἴποιμι. μιγείην is the aorist passive optative of μίγνυμι 'mix', 'join the company of', with the dative μνηστήρεσσιν ὑπερφιάλοισι, 'the overweening suitors'. εἴ μοι δεῖπνον δοῖεν is 'if they would give me a meal'; ὀνείατα 'good things to eat' is a rare neuter plural, here with μυρία 'countless'.

sentences.t: αἶψά κεν εὖ δρώοιμι μετὰ σφίσιν ἅσσ’ ἐθέλοιεν.
sentences.tr: aipsa ken eu drōoimi meta sphisin hass’ etheloien.
sentences.l: Quickly I could do well, among them, whatever they might wish.
sentences.i: I could quickly serve them well, whatever they might wish.
sentences.n: αἶψα 'quickly'. δρώοιμι is the optative of δράω 'do, act', which also means 'serve'; with εὖ it says 'I could do my work well'. μετὰ σφίσιν is 'among them', σφίσι being the dative of the plural pronoun. ἅσσ’ is ἅσσα, the same as ἅτινα 'whatever', and ἐθέλοιεν an indefinite optative, 'they might wish'.

sentences.t: ἐκ γάρ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δὲ σύνθεο καί μευ ἄκουσον·
sentences.tr: ek gar toi ereō, sy de syntheo kai meu akouson·
sentences.l: For I will speak out to you, and you, take it in, and hear me:
sentences.i: For I will tell it out to you plainly, and you must take it in and hear me:
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἐρέω is tmesis: ἐκ with ἐρέω gives 'I will speak out', and ἐρέω is a future of εἶπον. τοι is 'to you'. σύνθεο is the aorist imperative middle of συντίθημι 'put together (in the mind), take in'. ἄκουσον 'hear' takes the genitive μευ, as verbs of hearing do, 'hear me'. The unit ends at the Greek ano teleia, shown as a colon in English, since what he will tell comes next.

sentences.t:
Ἑρμείαο ἕκητι διακτόρου, ὅς ῥά τε πάντων
ἀνθρώπων ἔργοισι χάριν καὶ κῦδος ὀπάζει,
sentences.tr:
Hermeiao hekēti diaktorou, hos rha te pantōn
anthrōpōn ergoisi charin kai kydos opazei,
sentences.l:
By the will of Hermes, the guide, who indeed, of all
men, upon their works grace and glory bestows,
sentences.i: By the will of Hermes the guide, who bestows grace and glory on the work of all men,
sentences.n: Ἑρμείαο is the genitive in -αο of Ἑρμείας 'Hermes'; ἕκητι, 'by the will of', takes the genitive. The meaning of διάκτορος is not known: 'guide' is the traditional guess, here a title of Hermes. ὅς ῥά τε: τε after a relative marks a truth that holds always, 'who (as is always so) bestows'. ὀπάζει 'bestow, grant'; χάριν καὶ κῦδος 'grace and glory'; ἔργοισι is a dative plural, 'upon the works', and πάντων ἀνθρώπων 'of all men' belongs with it.

sentences.t:
δρηστοσύνῃ οὐκ ἄν μοι ἐρίσσειε βροτὸς ἄλλος,
πῦρ τ’ εὖ νηῆσαι διά τε ξύλα δανὰ κεάσσαι,
δαιτρεῦσαί τε καὶ ὀπτῆσαι καὶ οἰνοχοῆσαι,
οἷά τε τοῖς ἀγαθοῖσι παραδρώωσι χέρηες.
sentences.tr:
drēstosynēi ouk an moi erisseie brotos allos,
pyr t’ eu nēēsai dia te xyla dana keassai,
daitreusai te kai optēsai kai oinochoēsai,
hoia te tois agathoisi paradrōōsi cherēes.
sentences.l:
in service could not rival me another mortal,
both to heap a fire well and to split dry logs through,
to carve and to roast and to pour wine,
such things as for the good do service the lesser.”
sentences.i: no other mortal could rival me in service, at building up a fire well and splitting dry logs, at carving and roasting and pouring wine, at all the things that lesser men do for their betters.”
sentences.n: δρηστοσύνῃ 'in service' is a dative of respect, from the noun built on δράω. οὐκ ἄν … ἐρίσσειε is the optative of ἐρίζω 'vie', 'could not vie with me' (μοι); βροτὸς ἄλλος 'another mortal'. The infinitives in the lines after say in what: νηῆσαι 'to heap up', διὰ … κεάσσαι (tmesis for διακεάσσαι) 'to split through', ξύλα δανά 'dry logs' (δανός is 'dry' by the traditional gloss, sense uncertain), δαιτρεῦσαι 'to carve meat', ὀπτῆσαι 'to roast', οἰνοχοῆσαι 'to pour wine'. οἷά τε is 'such things as'; παραδρώωσι is 'do service beside', and χέρηες is the nominative plural of χέρης, 'lesser, inferior', set against τοῖς ἀγαθοῖσι 'the good', that is, men of rank. This unit ends the speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.tr: ton de meg’ ochthēsas prosephēs, Eumaie sybōta·
sentences.l: Him then, greatly vexed, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: Then, greatly troubled, you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: τὸν δέ is 'and him'. μέγ’ is μέγα, 'greatly', adverbial, with ὀχθήσας, the aorist participle of ὀχθέω 'be vexed, troubled'. προσέφης is second person: the poet turns to Eumaeus and speaks to him directly ('you addressed'), where a speech-formula would ordinarily have 'he'. Εὔμαιε συβῶτα is the vocative of the name with the title συβώτης 'swineherd'.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι, ξεῖνε, τίη τοι ἐνὶ φρεσὶ τοῦτο νόημα
ἔπλετο;
sentences.tr:
ō moi, xeine, tiē toi eni phresi touto noēma
epleto;
sentences.l:
“Oh me, stranger, why to you in your mind this thought
has arisen?
sentences.i: “Oh me, stranger, why has this notion come into your mind?
sentences.n: ὤ μοι is the cry 'oh me', one of dismay. τίη is 'why'; τοι is 'to you'; ἐνὶ φρεσί 'in your mind' (ἐνί is ἐν, φρεσί the dative plural of φρένες). νόημα 'thought, purpose'. ἔπλετο is the aorist of πέλομαι 'come to be', 'has arisen'. The unit stops in the middle of line 327.

sentences.t: ἦ σύ γε πάγχυ λιλαίεαι αὐτόθ’ ὀλέσθαι.
sentences.tr: ē sy ge panchy lilaieai autoth’ olesthai.
sentences.l: Truly you altogether are longing to perish right there.
sentences.i: Surely you long outright to perish on the spot.
sentences.n: ἦ 'truly' and σύ γε 'you at least' give the sentence its force. πάγχυ 'altogether'. λιλαίεαι is λιλαίομαι 'long for' in its uncontracted -εαι form, with the aorist infinitive ὀλέσθαι 'to perish' (ὄλλυμι). αὐτόθ’ is αὐτόθι 'right there, on the spot', that is, among the suitors.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὴ μνηστήρων ἐθέλεις καταδῦναι ὅμιλον,
τῶν ὕβρις τε βίη τε σιδήρεον οὐρανὸν ἵκει.
sentences.tr:
ei dē mnēstērōn etheleis katadynai homilon,
tōn hybris te biē te sidēreon ouranon hikei.
sentences.l:
If indeed to plunge into the throng of suitors you wish,
whose both insolence and violence the iron heaven reaches.
sentences.i: If you truly want to plunge into the throng of the suitors, whose insolence and violence reach the iron sky.
sentences.n: εἰ δή is 'if indeed'. καταδῦναι is the aorist infinitive of καταδύω 'go down into, plunge into', with the object ὅμιλον 'throng'. τῶν is 'of whom', the pronoun used as a relative. ὕβρις and βίη 'insolence' and 'violence' are the subjects of ἵκει 'reaches'. σιδήρεον οὐρανόν 'the iron heaven' pictures the sky as a vault of hard metal, so the words say that the suitors' insolence and violence have risen as high as it can go.

sentences.t:
οὔ τοι τοιοίδ’ εἰσὶν ὑποδρηστῆρες ἐκείνων,
ἀλλὰ νέοι, χλαίνας εὖ εἱμένοι ἠδὲ χιτῶνας,
αἰεὶ δὲ λιπαροὶ κεφαλὰς καὶ καλὰ πρόσωπα,
οἵ σφιν ὑποδρώωσιν·
sentences.tr:
ou toi toioid’ eisin hypodrēstēres ekeinōn,
alla neoi, chlainas eu heimenoi ēde chitōnas,
aiei de liparoi kephalas kai kala prosōpa,
hoi sphin hypodrōōsin·
sentences.l:
Not at all such as this are the serving-men of those men,
but young men, well clothed in cloaks and tunics,
and always sleek as to heads and fine faces,
who serve them;
sentences.i: Their serving-men are not such as you, but young men, well clothed in cloaks and tunics, always sleek of head and with beautiful faces, who wait on them;
sentences.n: οὔ τοι is 'not at all'. τοιοίδ’ is 'such as this', and points at the beggar, 'such as you'. ὑποδρηστῆρες 'serving-men' is built on ὑπό 'under' + δράω, as the verb ὑποδρώωσιν at the end of the unit is: 'who serve'. ἐκείνων 'of those men', the suitors. εὖ εἱμένοι is the perfect middle participle of ἕννυμι 'clothe', 'well clothed', with the accusatives χλαίνας ἠδὲ χιτῶνας 'in cloaks and tunics'. λιπαροὶ κεφαλάς: λιπαρός is 'sleek' (as if rubbed with oil), and κεφαλάς and πρόσωπα are accusatives of respect, 'as to heads and faces'. The unit stops in the middle of line 333.

sentences.t:
ἐΰξεστοι δὲ τράπεζαι
σίτου καὶ κρειῶν ἠδ’ οἴνου βεβρίθασιν.
sentences.tr:
eÿxestoi de trapezai
sitou kai kreiōn ēd’ oinou bebrithasin.
sentences.l:
and well-polished tables
with food and meats and wine are weighed down.
sentences.i: and the well-polished tables are weighed down with food and meat and wine.
sentences.n: ἐΰξεστοι is 'well-polished' (ἐΰ- 'well' + ξέω 'plane, polish'); τράπεζαι 'tables'. βεβρίθασιν is the perfect of βρίθω 'be heavy', 'are weighed down', with genitives of what weighs them: σίτου 'food', κρειῶν (a form of κρεῶν) 'meat', οἴνου 'wine'.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ μέν’·
sentences.tr: alla men’·
sentences.l: But stay;
sentences.i: No, stay;
sentences.n: μέν’ is μένε, the imperative of μένω 'stay', with its vowel elided. ἀλλά is 'but, no'. The unit is only these two words because the Greek text closes the thought here with an ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τίς τοι ἀνιᾶται παρεόντι,
οὔτ’ ἐγὼ οὔτε τις ἄλλος ἑταίρων, οἵ μοι ἔασιν.
sentences.tr:
ou gar tis toi aniatai pareonti,
out’ egō oute tis allos hetairōn, hoi moi easin.
sentences.l:
for not anyone is distressed at you being present,
neither I nor any other of the companions who are mine.
sentences.i: for no one is distressed at your presence, neither I nor any other of the companions I have.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for staying. ἀνιᾶται 'is distressed' (ἀνιάομαι, from ἀνίη 'distress') takes the dative participle παρεόντι, 'at you being present' (πάρειμι 'be present'). οὔτ’ ἐγὼ οὔτε τις ἄλλος ἑταίρων is 'neither I nor any other of the companions', a partitive genitive; οἵ μοι ἔασιν 'who are mine', ἔασιν being the epic third plural of εἰμί, with μοι of possession.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν ἔλθῃσιν Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός,
κεῖνός σε χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματα ἕσσει,
πέμψει δ’ ὅππη σε κραδίη θυμός τε κελεύει.
sentences.tr:
autar epēn elthēisin Odyssēos philos huios,
keinos se chlainan te chitōna te heimata hessei,
pempsei d’ hoppē se kradiē thymos te keleuei.
sentences.l:
But when there has come Odysseus’ dear son,
that one will clothe you with a cloak and a tunic, clothes,
and will send you wherever heart and spirit bid.”
sentences.i: But when the dear son of Odysseus has come, he will put a cloak and a tunic about you for clothing, and will send you wherever your heart and spirit bid you.”
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπήν: ἐπήν is ἐπεί + ἄν, 'when', with the aorist subjunctive ἔλθῃσιν (a third singular with the old ending -ῃσιν). Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός is the fixed phrase for Telemachus, 'Odysseus’ dear son'. κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος 'that one'. ἕσσει is the future of ἕννυμι 'clothe', with two accusatives, 'will clothe you with a cloak and a tunic'. ὅππῃ is 'where, whither' (Attic ὅπῃ). κραδίη 'heart' and θυμός 'spirit' stand together, and the English keeps the two words apart. This unit ends the speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita polytlas dios Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him then answered much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus answered him:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα is the reply-formula 'then answered him'; ἠμείβετο is the imperfect middle of ἀμείβομαι 'reply', and the formula is kept apart from the 'addressed' formulas by this verb. πολύτλας (πολύ + τλῆναι 'endure') and δῖος are epithets of Odysseus, 'much-enduring' and 'heavenly', translated each time.

sentences.t:
αἴθ’ οὕτως, Εὔμαιε, φίλος Διὶ πατρὶ γένοιο
ὡς ἐμοί, ὅττι μ’ ἔπαυσας ἄλης καὶ ὀϊζύος αἰνῆς.
sentences.tr:
aith’ houtōs, Eumaie, philos Dii patri genoio
hōs emoi, hotti m’ epausas alēs kai oïzyos ainēs.
sentences.l:
“Would that thus, Eumaeus, dear to Father Zeus you might become
as to me, because you made me cease from wandering and fearsome distress.
sentences.i: “If only, Eumaeus, you might become as dear to Father Zeus as you are to me, since you have made me cease from wandering and from fearsome distress.
sentences.n: αἴθ’ is αἴθε 'would that', a wish with the optative γένοιο 'might you become'. φίλος Διὶ πατρί is 'dear to Father Zeus', the dative of the one to whom someone is dear; ὡς ἐμοί 'as (you are) to me'. ὅττι is ὅτι 'because'. ἔπαυσας is the aorist of παύω 'make cease', and a verb of ceasing takes the genitive of what ceases: ἄλης 'wandering' (related to ἀλάομαι) and ὀϊζύος 'distress'. αἰνῆς is 'fearsome'.

sentences.t: πλαγκτοσύνης δ’ οὐκ ἔστι κακώτερον ἄλλο βροτοῖσιν·
sentences.tr: planktosynēs d’ ouk esti kakōteron allo brotoisin·
sentences.l: And than straying there is no other thing worse for mortals;
sentences.i: And there is nothing worse for mortals than roaming;
sentences.n: πλαγκτοσύνης is a genitive of comparison, 'than straying', governed by the comparative κακώτερον 'worse'; the noun is built on πλάζομαι 'be driven off course, stray'. οὐκ ἔστι … ἄλλο 'there is not another thing'. βροτοῖσιν is a dative, 'for mortals'. The line is a general saying, and the ano teleia closes it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἕνεκ’ οὐλομένης γαστρὸς κακὰ κήδε’ ἔχουσιν
ἀνέρες, ὅν τιν’ ἵκηται ἄλη καὶ πῆμα καὶ ἄλγος.
sentences.tr:
all’ henek’ oulomenēs gastros kaka kēde’ echousin
aneres, hon tin’ hikētai alē kai pēma kai algos.
sentences.l:
but for the sake of the ruinous belly evil sorrows have
men, whomever wandering and woe and pain may reach.
sentences.i: Yet for the sake of the ruinous belly men have evil sorrows, any man whom wandering and woe and pain come upon.
sentences.n: ἀλλά is 'but, yet': after saying nothing is worse than straying, Odysseus says what drives men to it. ἕνεκ’ is ἕνεκα 'for the sake of', with οὐλομένης γαστρός 'the ruinous belly'; οὐλόμενος is a word of cursing, 'ruinous, accursed'. κακὰ κήδεα 'evil sorrows'. ὅν τιν’ ἵκηται is 'whomever may reach', with the aorist subjunctive; its three subjects are ἄλη 'wandering', πῆμα 'woe', ἄλγος 'pain'.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἐπεὶ ἰσχανάᾳς μεῖναί τέ με κεῖνον ἄνωγας,
sentences.tr: nyn d’ epei ischanaāis meinai te me keinon anōgas,
sentences.l: But now, since you are holding me back and bid me wait for that one,
sentences.i: But now, since you hold me back and tell me to wait for him,
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ἐπεί is 'but now since'. ἰσχανάᾳς is a rare lengthened form of ἰσχάνω 'hold back', and its sense here is not certain: 'you hold me back', or 'you are eager (to keep me)'. ἄνωγας is a perfect with present sense, 'you bid, urge'. μεῖναι is the aorist infinitive of μένω, which with an accusative means 'wait for'; κεῖνον is ἐκεῖνον 'that man', Telemachus. The unit ends at a comma, because the request itself fills the next four lines.

sentences.t:
εἴπ’ ἄγε μοι περὶ μητρὸς Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο
πατρός θ’, ὃν κατέλειπεν ἰὼν ἐπὶ γήραος οὐδῷ,
ἤ που ἔτι ζώουσιν ὑπ’ αὐγὰς ἠελίοιο,
ἦ ἤδη τεθνᾶσι καὶ εἰν Ἀΐδαο δόμοισι.
sentences.tr:
eip’ age moi peri mētros Odyssēos theioio
patros th’, hon kateleipen iōn epi gēraos oudōi,
ē pou eti zōousin hyp’ augas ēelioio,
ē ēdē tethnasi kai ein Aïdao domoisi.
sentences.l:
tell me, come, about the mother of divine Odysseus
and the father, whom he left, going, on the threshold of old age,
whether perhaps still they live beneath the rays of the sun,
or already are dead and in the house of Hades.”
sentences.i: Come, tell me about the mother of divine Odysseus, and about his father, whom he left on the threshold of old age when he went away: whether they are perhaps still living beneath the rays of the sun, or are already dead and in the house of Hades.”
sentences.n: εἴπ’ ἄγε μοι is 'tell me, come'. περὶ μητρὸς … πατρός θ’ is 'about the mother … and the father': Odysseus, still in disguise, asks about his own parents, as of strangers. κατέλειπεν is the imperfect of καταλείπω 'leave behind'; ἰών 'going' is the participle of εἶμι. γήραος οὐδῷ is 'on the threshold of old age', οὐδός being the threshold. ἤ … ἦ is 'whether … or' in an indirect question; που 'perhaps'; ζώουσιν is the uncontracted form of ζώω 'live'. ὑπ’ αὐγὰς ἠελίοιο is 'beneath the rays of the sun', ἠελίοιο a genitive in -οιο. τεθνᾶσι is the perfect of θνῄσκω, 'they are dead'; εἰν is ἐν; Ἀΐδαο is the genitive of Ἀΐδης 'Hades'. This unit ends the speech.
